title: Shocker in the Deep South: How Mississippi’s Senate Race Turned Into a Razor-Thin Standoff
snippet: In what was projected as an easy Republican win in deep-red Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom holds a microscopic lead over incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith as final votes are tallied.
content:
JACKSON, Miss. — In one of the most unexpected twists of the 2026 midterm cycle, deep-red Mississippi has become the epicenter of national political suspense. What was widely expected to be a routine reelection win for Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith has transformed into a high-stakes thriller, with Democratic challenger Scott Colom clinging to a paper-thin lead as remaining ballots are counted.

As of late Thursday, Colom led Hyde-Smith by a mere 1,724 votes out of nearly one million cast — a razor-thin margin of just 0.19%. The Associated Press has held off on declaring a winner with roughly 96% of the vote tallied, keeping the political world glued to a contest few expected to be competitive in a state Donald Trump won by 23 percentage points in 2024.

A Personal Rivalry Comes Full Circle

Colom, 43, is a historic figure in Mississippi legal circles. In 2015, he became the first Black district attorney elected to represent a majority-white district in state history. His political profile rose nationally in 2022 when President Joe Biden nominated him to serve as a federal judge for the Northern District of Mississippi — a nomination initially endorsed by top Magnolia State Republicans.

However, Hyde-Smith used her Senate power to block his nomination, pointing to past campaign donations from a political action committee linked to billionaire George Soros and accusing Colom of holding progressive views on culture-war issues. After his nomination was formally returned to the White House in 2024, Colom launched his Senate campaign the following year, setting up a direct rematch at the ballot box.

The Viral Ad That Flipped the Script

For months, national race raters categorized the contest as a comfortable Republican hold, and polling was scarce. But the trajectory of the race dramatically shifted in mid-October following a tone-deaf response from Hyde-Smith regarding rising consumer prices.

When questioned by a local television station about high beef prices, Hyde-Smith minimized the issue, remarking that "all commodities go through peaks and valleys" and pointing out that shoppers have "so many proteins to choose from."

Colom’s team swiftly capitalized on the remark, producing a viral video ad featuring everyday Mississippians scoffing at the "proteins" comment while shopping for groceries and grilling in their backyards. The video racked up nearly 14 million views online, unleashing a wave of national Democratic enthusiasm and financial backing. Heavyweights including former Presidents Barack Obama and Bill Clinton, along with Vice President Kamala Harris, jumped into the fray to campaign for Colom, forcing national Republicans into emergency defensive mode.

The Final Count and Potential Legal Fights

The outcome now hinges on outstanding mail-in ballots and thousands of provisional affidavit ballots cast across several key counties. County clerks have until Nov. 13 to certify official results.

Colom’s campaign expressed optimism that the remaining uncounted ballots, particularly affidavit votes stemming from voter registration list discrepancies earlier in the year, would expand his lead. Meanwhile, Hyde-Smith’s legal team has already sent formal demands to state election officials demanding the preservation of all affidavit ballots — a clear sign that legal challenges could follow if the margin stays incredibly tight.

Because Mississippi is the only state in the nation without a statutory recount law, any challenge to the certified results will likely play out in state courts after the final deadline next week.
